items.bodyEn: Yui sat below Satta Pass, where the mountains drop into Suruga Bay. The oldest route ran along the beach beneath the cliffs and was passable only at low tide. A path over the pass was cut in 1655, ahead of a Korean embassy's journey to Edo. Hiroshige's print shows travellers peering down at Fuji from that cliffside road.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, 'Yui: Satta Pass' (Hōeidō ed., 1833–34); Tōkaidō Meisho Zue (1797)

items.bodyEn: The pass's name is Buddhist. Satta transliterates Sanskrit sattva, 'a being', and is the second half of bodai-satta, 'enlightenment-being', the full form of bosatsu, bodhisattva. The two kanji were chosen for their sound rather than their meaning, which is why the second one hardly appears anywhere else in modern Japanese.
items.sourceNote: Kōjien and Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, entries 薩埵・菩提薩埵

items.bodyEn: In casual speech 〜てしまう shrinks to 〜ちゃう, or 〜じゃう after a voiced て-form: たべてしまった becomes たべちゃった, よんでしまった becomes よんじゃった. Likewise 〜ておく becomes 〜とく: かっとく, やっとく. The short forms keep the same meanings, completion or regret for しまう and preparation for おく, but they belong to friends and family; use the full forms in writing and polite speech.

Fukusui bon ni kaerazu: spilled water does not go back into the tray. It comes from a Chinese anecdote about a scholar whose wife left him in poverty and asked to return once he rose; he spilled water and told her to put it back. Use it where English says what's done is done, the mood 〜てしまう often carries.
items.ja: {覆水|ふくすい}{盆|ぼん}に{返|かえ}らず。
items.kana: ふくすいぼんにかえらず。
